Linguistic Principles for Foundation Models

Table Serialization Determines
Which Relations Language Models Preserve

Junwei Ma  Arun Kumar Chithanar  Palash Goyal  Chul Lee ††thanks: Corresponding author: junweima2@gmail.com Affiliation: University of Toronto
Abstract

We study how text serialization affects table lookup in instruction-tuned language models. Our diagnostic asks the model to find the row containing a specified value under one named column, then return the value under another named column in that same row. We render the same synthetic 256-cell tables in row-major form and in column-major form with each header placed beside its values, while varying the table aspect ratio across five shapes. Across three models, the better format changes with table shape: row-major performs better on tall tables, whereas column-major performs better on wide tables. At 64×464\times 4, row-major leads by 42.3–54.0 percentage points; at 4×644\times 64, column-major leads by 35.0–59.0 points. Mapping wrong answers back to their source cells reveals a complementary error pattern: row-major tends to preserve the correct row but lose the target column, while column-major tends to preserve the correct column but lose the row. We use the term relational locality to describe this pattern: serialization keeps one relation locally available while making the other depend on positional alignment. A separate non-tabular ordering experiment supports this interpretation. Thus, apparent width-related failures in text-serialized tables depend on linearization, not table shape alone.

1 Introduction

Tables are a common way to organize information in spreadsheets, databases, reports, and software tools. General-purpose language models are increasingly asked to answer questions over such data (Sui et al., 2023; Liu et al., 2024b; Jiang et al., 2023). When a table is included in a text prompt, however, it must be written as a sequence—usually row by row or column by column. These renderings can contain exactly the same cells while placing different labels and values next to one another.

Under the common row-major format, accuracy on some table tasks falls as more columns are added. This observation alone does not show that wide tables are inherently difficult: adding columns also lengthens every serialized row and increases the distance between the header and its values. Table shape and serialization are therefore confounded. A controlled comparison must hold the table itself fixed while changing how it is written.

We make this comparison using a simple lookup task. The model is told that a particular value appears in one named column and must return the value from a different named column in the same row. We render the same synthetic 256-cell tables in row-major and locally headed column-major form, vary their aspect ratio across five shapes, and evaluate three instruction-tuned language models. Because the cell contents, question, and answer are unchanged within each pair, differences in accuracy can be attributed to the representation.

The better representation changes with table shape. Row-major text performs better on tall tables, whereas column-major text performs better on wide tables. The errors also reverse: row-major predictions more often retain the correct row but miss the requested column, while column-major predictions more often retain the correct column but miss the row. We call this pattern relational locality: a serialization makes some relations easier to recover by keeping their relevant values and labels together. This motivates a simple hypothesis: language models recover a relation more reliably when the serialization keeps those elements together. We test it through a paired row-versus-column lookup experiment and a separate non-tabular ordering experiment. Our main conclusion is that apparent width-related failures in text-serialized tables depend on linearization as well as table shape.

2 Experiments

2.1 Row-major versus column-major lookup

Task.

Each synthetic table has named columns and unique values. The question identifies a row by giving a known value in one column, then asks for the value in a different column from that same row. Let T∈𝒱R×CT\in\mathcal{V}^{R\times C} contain unique values. A query supplies a predicate (cp,vp)(c_{p},v_{p}) that determines row rr through Tr,cp=vpT_{r,c_{p}}=v_{p}, and a different target column ctc_{t}. The answer is Tr,ctT_{r,c_{t}}. Crossover prompts add no row labels, although their predicate values use a distinct type.

The lookup is semantically equivalent to the following database query (we do not execute SQL):

SELECT Salary
FROM employees
WHERE Employee = ’Bob’;

Figure 1 shows the two natural text renderings used in the main comparison. All paired prompts contain exactly the same logical table, display-column order, question, and answer.

Hypothesis.

The relational locality hypothesis predicts that a format will favor the relation it keeps together. Row-major keeps rows together but requires a global header-to-position mapping; locally headed column-major keeps each header beside its values but requires alignment across columns. We therefore predict that added columns will hurt row-major, whereas added rows will hurt column-major.

Protocol.

We test five 256-cell shapes from ×464\!\times\!4 to ×644\!\times\!64, with 300 paired tables per shape and 3,000 prompts per model. We evaluate two Qwen 3B models and Phi-3.5 Mini with greedy decoding (Hui et al., 2024; Yang et al., 2024; Abdin et al., 2024). Exact accuracy requires the target cell; Figure 3 additionally checks whether a wrong value comes from the correct row or requested column. Error bars are Wilson 95% intervals. Full generation, parsing, and inference details are in Appendix A.

Accuracy crossover.

Figure 2 shows the crossover in all three models. Row-major dominates at the two tall shapes, the curves approach one another near square, and locally headed column-major dominates at the two wide shapes. At 64×464\times 4, column-minus-row differences range from −42.3-42.3 to −54.0-54.0 points; at 4×644\times 64, they range from +35.0+35.0 to +59.0+59.0 points (Appendix Table 1). The paired differences directly show that the representation advantage reverses between the tallest and widest shapes, as relational locality predicts.

Valid-value extraction is 95.3–98.3% for the Qwen models and 99.0–100% for Phi, so output truncation cannot explain the interaction. The predictions are mostly wrong cells from the displayed table.

Where wrong answers come from.

Figure 3 checks whether each valid prediction comes from the correct row or the requested column. The errors are not undifferentiated retrieval failures. For Qwen Coder at 4×644\times 64, row-major retains the correct row in 69.0% of prompts but the correct column in only 4.0%, producing 2.7% exact accuracy. At the transposed aspect ratio, 64×464\times 4 column-major retains the correct column in 77.0% but the correct row in only 7.0%, producing 6.7% exact accuracy. The corresponding random-valid-cell baselines are 25% for the shorter dimension and 1.6% for the longer dimension. The same reversal appears in the other checkpoints. Serialization therefore preserves one dimension while making the other fragile. Individual outputs exhibit the same distinction: a wide row-major error can select another field from the identified record, while a tall column-major error can select the requested field from a different record. Together with the crossover, this reversal in where errors come from is the main evidence for relational locality in table lookup.

Appendix C reports an independent-axis replication and additional serialization ablations.

2.2 Non-tabular pairwise intersection: grouped versus interleaved

Task.

To test whether relational locality extends beyond table coordinates, we construct a sequence of labeled GROUP=VALUE records. Every pair of groups shares exactly one unique value, and the model must identify the value shared by the two groups named in the question.

Example.

A simplified three-group instance makes the ordering change concrete:

Grouped order: Red=apple | Red=violin | Red=cloud
Blue=apple | Blue=river | Blue=lamp
Green=violin | Green=river | Green=chair

Two-fragment order: Red=apple | Red=violin | Blue=apple | Blue=river
Green=violin | Green=river | Red=cloud | Blue=lamp | Green=chair

Interleaved order: Red=cloud | Blue=apple | Green=violin | Red=violin
Blue=river | Green=river | Red=apple | Blue=lamp | Green=chair

Question: Which value occurs in both Red and Blue? Answer: apple.

All versions contain the same records. A fragment is one uninterrupted group block, so each group has one, two, or three above. In the middle order, Red’s two fragments are Red=apple | Red=violin and Red=cloud. The experiment uses four groups and longer numeric lists.

Hypothesis.

The relational locality hypothesis predicts that keeping a queried group together makes its shared value easier to recover, even without table rows or columns. Accuracy should therefore fall as the same records are split into more fragments.

Protocol.

For 100 base instances at each of 8 and 16 values per group, we render 1, 2, 4, 8, or 16 fragments, yielding 900 prompts. Paired conditions keep the records, tokens, question, and answer fixed. We evaluate Qwen2.5-Coder-3B-Instruct with greedy decoding and exact-match scoring. Error bars are Wilson 95% intervals; contrasts use paired bootstrap intervals. Full details are in Appendix A.

Results.

With 8 values per group, accuracy falls from 36% with one fragment to 24% under full interleaving; with 16, it falls from 33% to 11% (Figure 2.2). Across lengths, one fragment adds 17.0 points over full interleaving (95% paired CI [9.0,25.0][9.0,25.0]), and each fragmentation doubling costs 5.2 points ([2.6,7.6][2.6,7.6]). Because content is fixed, this supports relational locality beyond table coordinates.

3 Related work

Table-aware language models encode structure directly (Herzig et al., 2020; Yin et al., 2020; Liu et al., 2022), while tabular foundation models target supervised numerical prediction (Hollmann et al., 2025; Ma et al., 2025; Qu et al., 2025). We instead study an unmodified instruction-tuned model receiving tables as text. Prior work shows that serialization, structural perturbations, and structured-data interfaces affect language-model performance (Sui et al., 2023; Singha et al., 2023; Liu et al., 2024b; Sui et al., 2024; Jiang et al., 2023; Dong et al., 2024; Li et al., 2025), and that retrieval is position-sensitive (Liu et al., 2024a). Our paired design holds the logical table and query fixed, traces wrong values to source cells, and tests the same locality prediction in a non-tabular ordering task.

4 Discussion and limitations

Together, the experiments support relational locality: models more reliably recover relations kept close and grouped in the serialized prompt. The row–column crossover therefore is not evidence that width alone makes a table difficult: the formats move different relations into local spans, and the errors move with them. Serialization is part of the model-facing representation; when text is necessary, the format should keep the task-relevant relation local. Exact production table retrieval should still use SQL or dataframes when possible (Jiang et al., 2023). Our evidence uses synthetic, unique-valued inputs and two narrow diagnostic tasks; only the crossover spans three models, while the ordering study uses one. We identify no mechanism, did not preregister, and leave natural tables and other tasks open.

Appendix A Detailed experimental protocols

For lookup, prompts use native chat templates, pinned revisions, bfloat16 weights, greedy decoding, no demonstrations or training, and a 64-token cap. We extract the first generated six-digit value that occurs in the table. Exact accuracy requires the target cell; a valid wrong value receives row credit if it lies in the target row and column credit if it lies in the requested column. There are no response-based exclusions, and no retained completion exceeds 10 tokens. Wilson intervals summarize conditions; representation contrasts use 10,000 paired bootstrap resamples over logical tables and exact McNemar tests.

For pairwise intersection, each base instance has four groups and one unique shared value per group pair. The 900 prompts cover 100 instances at each of 8 and 16 values per group; paired versions have identical records, values, questions, answers, prompt length, and tokenizer multiset. Qwen2.5-Coder-3B-Instruct uses its native chat template, bfloat16 weights, greedy decoding, no demonstrations or training, and a 30-token cap. We extract the first generated six-digit value and require the value shared by the queried groups. There are no response-based exclusions, no completion exceeds six tokens, and contrasts use paired bootstrap intervals.

Appendix B Protocol audit and deviations

The original confirmatory document prespecified a Mistral-7B checkpoint as the third model. The executed run instead used Phi-3.5-mini-instruct. We report Phi as an additional cross-family replication but do not describe the executed three-model list as preregistered.

The same document prespecified a coordinate-label factorial. A post-run audit found that it repeated the predicate value beside every cell, effectively creating a row identifier, and that its column-major form did not preserve the locally headed grammar. We therefore exclude that factorial from every claim and figure. Its raw outputs remain in the artifact for provenance. The replacement independent-axis grid removes the repeated row descriptor but retains a type-distinguished predicate field, so we report it only as a replication and ablation rather than as confirmatory evidence.

Appendix C Additional lookup results

Table 1 gives the paired numerical contrasts behind the main crossover figure.

Figure 5 reports all 16 shapes in the separately generated grid. Pooled row-major/global-header, column-major/global-header, and column-major/local-header accuracies are 34.0%, 6.0%, and 36.4%, respectively. The near-zero pooled difference between the two operational formats (+2.3+2.3 points, CI [−0.2,4.9][-0.2,4.9]) conceals the predicted crossover: at 4×324\times 32, local column-major scores 58.0% versus 8.0% row-major, while at 32×432\times 4, row-major scores 52.0% versus 21.3% local column-major.

An odds ratio below one means that doubling an axis reduces the odds of a correct answer. Direct clustered interaction tests confirm that the operational representations have different slopes for rows (interaction OR 0.51, p<10−26p<10^{-26}) and columns (OR 1.75, p<10−18p<10^{-18}).

Appendix D Exact prompt templates

Discovery row prompts declare a global column order and render one value list per row. Global column prompts render one positional list per column; local column prompts render Column HjH_{j}: v1​jv_{1j} | …\ldots. All end with the exact question and answer-only instruction in Figure 1.

Fragmentation prompts render a sequence of individually labeled GROUP=VALUE records and ask: Find the only value that occurs in both group G1 and group G2. Every condition repeats the same answer-only instruction and 30-token response limit. Within a paired base instance, only record order changes.

Appendix E Reproducibility details

The constant-cell seed is 2026081801 and the independent-grid seed is 2026081502. The fragmentation dose response uses 20260825. The Qwen Coder revision is 488639f1ff808d1d3d0ba301aef8c11461451ec5; Qwen 3B uses aa8e72537993ba99e69dfaafa59ed015b17504d1; Phi-3.5 Mini uses 2fe192450127e6a83f7441aef6e3ca586c338b77. The Qwen checkpoints are distributed under the Qwen Research License and Phi-3.5 Mini under the MIT License; the pinned model cards are https://huggingface.co/Qwen/Qwen2.5-Coder-3B-Instruct, https://huggingface.co/Qwen/Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct, and https://huggingface.co/microsoft/Phi-3.5-mini-instruct.

All reported generation ran on RunPod RTX 4090 instances with 24 GB memory. The three crossover runs took 9, 12, and 17 minutes, and the independent grid took 34 minutes. The ordering experiment ran on the same hardware; no training was performed. A complete artifact with generators, frozen manifests, exact prompts, raw responses, scoring outputs, paired analyses, token summaries, plots, GPU metadata, and SHA-256 checksums will be released after anonymous review.

NeurIPS Paper Checklist

  1. 1.

    Claims

  2. Question: Do the main claims made in the abstract and introduction accurately reflect the paper’s contributions and scope?

  3. Answer: [Yes]

  4. Justification: The abstract and Sections 1–2 state both tasks, the tested model scope, paired interventions, principal effect sizes, and the deliberately behavioral interpretation.

  5. Guidelines:

    • •

      The answer [N/A] means that the abstract and introduction do not include the claims made in the paper.

    • •

      The abstract and/or introduction should clearly state the claims made, including the contributions made in the paper and important assumptions and limitations. A [No] or [N/A] answer to this question will not be perceived well by the reviewers.

    • •

      The claims made should match theoretical and experimental results, and reflect how much the results can be expected to generalize to other settings.

    • •

      It is fine to include aspirational goals as motivation as long as it is clear that these goals are not attained by the paper.

  6. 2.

    Limitations

  7. Question: Does the paper discuss the limitations of the work performed by the authors?

  8. Answer: [Yes]

  9. Justification: Section 4 limits the claims to synthetic inputs, two narrow diagnostic tasks, three-model crossover evidence, and a one-model non-tabular ordering experiment; it also states that the study identifies no mechanism and was not preregistered.

  10. Guidelines:

    • •

      The answer [N/A] means that the paper has no limitation while the answer [No] means that the paper has limitations, but those are not discussed in the paper.

    • •

      The authors are encouraged to create a separate “Limitations” section in their paper.

    • •

      The paper should point out any strong assumptions and how robust the results are to violations of these assumptions (e.g., independence assumptions, noiseless settings, model well-specification, asymptotic approximations only holding locally). The authors should reflect on how these assumptions might be violated in practice and what the implications would be.

    • •

      The authors should reflect on the scope of the claims made, e.g., if the approach was only tested on a few datasets or with a few runs. In general, empirical results often depend on implicit assumptions, which should be articulated.

    • •

      The authors should reflect on the factors that influence the performance of the approach. For example, a facial recognition algorithm may perform poorly when image resolution is low or images are taken in low lighting. Or a speech-to-text system might not be used reliably to provide closed captions for online lectures because it fails to handle technical jargon.

    • •

      The authors should discuss the computational efficiency of the proposed algorithms and how they scale with dataset size.

    • •

      If applicable, the authors should discuss possible limitations of their approach to address problems of privacy and fairness.

    • •

      While the authors might fear that complete honesty about limitations might be used by reviewers as grounds for rejection, a worse outcome might be that reviewers discover limitations that aren’t acknowledged in the paper. The authors should use their best judgment and recognize that individual actions in favor of transparency play an important role in developing norms that preserve the integrity of the community. Reviewers will be specifically instructed to not penalize honesty concerning limitations.

  11. 3.

    Theory assumptions and proofs

  12. Question: For each theoretical result, does the paper provide the full set of assumptions and a complete (and correct) proof?

  13. Answer: [N/A]

  14. Justification: The paper reports behavioral experiments and statistical models, not theoretical results or proofs.

  15. Guidelines:

    • •

      The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not include theoretical results.

    • •

      All the theorems, formulas, and proofs in the paper should be numbered and cross-referenced.

    • •

      All assumptions should be clearly stated or referenced in the statement of any theorems.

    • •

      The proofs can either appear in the main paper or the supplemental material, but if they appear in the supplemental material, the authors are encouraged to provide a short proof sketch to provide intuition.

    • •

      Inversely, any informal proof provided in the core of the paper should be complemented by formal proofs provided in appendix or supplemental material.

    • •

      Theorems and Lemmas that the proof relies upon should be properly referenced.

  16. 4.

    Experimental result reproducibility

  17. Question: Does the paper fully disclose all the information needed to reproduce the main experimental results of the paper to the extent that it affects the main claims and/or conclusions of the paper (regardless of whether the code and data are provided or not)?

  18. Answer: [Yes]

  19. Justification: Section 2 and Appendices A–E specify generation, scoring, paired statistics, prompt templates, seeds, checkpoint revisions, protocol deviations, and compute.

  20. Guidelines:

    • •

      The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not include experiments.

    • •

      If the paper includes experiments, a [No] answer to this question will not be perceived well by the reviewers: Making the paper reproducible is important, regardless of whether the code and data are provided or not.

    • •

      If the contribution is a dataset and/or model, the authors should describe the steps taken to make their results reproducible or verifiable.

    • •

      Depending on the contribution, reproducibility can be accomplished in various ways. For example, if the contribution is a novel architecture, describing the architecture fully might suffice, or if the contribution is a specific model and empirical evaluation, it may be necessary to either make it possible for others to replicate the model with the same dataset, or provide access to the model. In general. releasing code and data is often one good way to accomplish this, but reproducibility can also be provided via detailed instructions for how to replicate the results, access to a hosted model (e.g., in the case of a large language model), releasing of a model checkpoint, or other means that are appropriate to the research performed.

    • •

      While NeurIPS does not require releasing code, the conference does require all submissions to provide some reasonable avenue for reproducibility, which may depend on the nature of the contribution. For example

      1. (a)

        If the contribution is primarily a new algorithm, the paper should make it clear how to reproduce that algorithm.

      2. (b)

        If the contribution is primarily a new model architecture, the paper should describe the architecture clearly and fully.

      3. (c)

        If the contribution is a new model (e.g., a large language model), then there should either be a way to access this model for reproducing the results or a way to reproduce the model (e.g., with an open-source dataset or instructions for how to construct the dataset).

      4. (d)

        We recognize that reproducibility may be tricky in some cases, in which case authors are welcome to describe the particular way they provide for reproducibility. In the case of closed-source models, it may be that access to the model is limited in some way (e.g., to registered users), but it should be possible for other researchers to have some path to reproducing or verifying the results.

  31. 7.

    Experiment statistical significance

  32. Question: Does the paper report error bars suitably and correctly defined or other appropriate information about the statistical significance of the experiments?

  33. Answer: [Yes]

  34. Justification: Sections 2.1–2.2 report Wilson 95% intervals over independently sampled prompts and paired bootstrap intervals for representation contrasts. Appendix A specifies 10,000 paired resamples and exact McNemar tests; Appendix C reports the clustered interaction analyses used for the additional grid.

  35. Guidelines:

    • •

      The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not include experiments.

    • •

      The authors should answer [Yes] if the results are accompanied by error bars, confidence intervals, or statistical significance tests, at least for the experiments that support the main claims of the paper.

    • •

      The factors of variability that the error bars are capturing should be clearly stated (for example, train/test split, initialization, random drawing of some parameter, or overall run with given experimental conditions).

    • •

      The method for calculating the error bars should be explained (closed form formula, call to a library function, bootstrap, etc.)

    • •

      The assumptions made should be given (e.g., Normally distributed errors).

    • •

      It should be clear whether the error bar is the standard deviation or the standard error of the mean.

    • •

      It is OK to report 1-sigma error bars, but one should state it. The authors should preferably report a 2-sigma error bar than state that they have a 96% CI, if the hypothesis of Normality of errors is not verified.

    • •

      For asymmetric distributions, the authors should be careful not to show in tables or figures symmetric error bars that would yield results that are out of range (e.g., negative error rates).

    • •

      If error bars are reported in tables or plots, the authors should explain in the text how they were calculated and reference the corresponding figures or tables in the text.

  36. 8.

    Experiments compute resources

  37. Question: For each experiment, does the paper provide sufficient information on the computer resources (type of compute workers, memory, time of execution) needed to reproduce the experiments?

  38. Answer: [No]

  39. Justification: Appendix E reports the RunPod RTX 4090 type, 24 GB memory, and durations for the three crossover runs and independent grid. The exact ordering-experiment duration and total development compute were not retained, so the disclosure is incomplete for this question’s standard.

  40. Guidelines:

    • •

      The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not include experiments.

    • •

      The paper should indicate the type of compute workers CPU or GPU, internal cluster, or cloud provider, including relevant memory and storage.

    • •

      The paper should provide the amount of compute required for each of the individual experimental runs as well as estimate the total compute.

    • •

      The paper should disclose whether the full research project required more compute than the experiments reported in the paper (e.g., preliminary or failed experiments that didn’t make it into the paper).

  41. 9.

    Code of ethics

  42. Question: Does the research conducted in the paper conform, in every respect, with the NeurIPS Code of Ethics https://neurips.cc/public/EthicsGuidelines?

  43. Answer: [Yes]

  44. Justification: The study uses synthetic tables and synthetic labeled-record sequences, openly distributed model checkpoints under their stated terms, and no personal, private, or human-subject data.

  45. Guidelines:

    • •

      The answer [N/A] means that the authors have not reviewed the NeurIPS Code of Ethics.

    • •

      If the authors answer [No] , they should explain the special circumstances that require a deviation from the Code of Ethics.

    • •

      The authors should make sure to preserve anonymity (e.g., if there is a special consideration due to laws or regulations in their jurisdiction).

  46. 10.

    Broader impacts

  47. Question: Does the paper discuss both potential positive societal impacts and negative societal impacts of the work performed?

  48. Answer: [N/A]

  49. Justification: This is a controlled diagnostic of text serialization with no direct deployment; Section 4 explicitly recommends deterministic SQL or dataframe execution for exact production table retrieval.

  50. Guidelines:

    • •

      The answer [N/A] means that there is no societal impact of the work performed.

    • •

      If the authors answer [N/A] or [No] , they should explain why their work has no societal impact or why the paper does not address societal impact.

    • •

      Examples of negative societal impacts include potential malicious or unintended uses (e.g., disinformation, generating fake profiles, surveillance), fairness considerations (e.g., deployment of technologies that could make decisions that unfairly impact specific groups), privacy considerations, and security considerations.

    • •

      The conference expects that many papers will be foundational research and not tied to particular applications, let alone deployments. However, if there is a direct path to any negative applications, the authors should point it out. For example, it is legitimate to point out that an improvement in the quality of generative models could be used to generate Deepfakes for disinformation. On the other hand, it is not needed to point out that a generic algorithm for optimizing neural networks could enable people to train models that generate Deepfakes faster.

    • •

      The authors should consider possible harms that could arise when the technology is being used as intended and functioning correctly, harms that could arise when the technology is being used as intended but gives incorrect results, and harms following from (intentional or unintentional) misuse of the technology.

    • •

      If there are negative societal impacts, the authors could also discuss possible mitigation strategies (e.g., gated release of models, providing defenses in addition to attacks, mechanisms for monitoring misuse, mechanisms to monitor how a system learns from feedback over time, improving the efficiency and accessibility of ML).

  51. 11.

    Safeguards

  52. Question: Does the paper describe safeguards that have been put in place for responsible release of data or models that have a high risk for misuse (e.g., pre-trained language models, image generators, or scraped datasets)?

  53. Answer: [N/A]

  54. Justification: The work releases neither a new model nor scraped or sensitive data, and the synthetic lookup artifacts do not create a material misuse risk.

  55. Guidelines:

    • •

      The answer [N/A] means that the paper poses no such risks.

    • •

      Released models that have a high risk for misuse or dual-use should be released with necessary safeguards to allow for controlled use of the model, for example by requiring that users adhere to usage guidelines or restrictions to access the model or implementing safety filters.

    • •

      Datasets that have been scraped from the Internet could pose safety risks. The authors should describe how they avoided releasing unsafe images.

    • •

      We recognize that providing effective safeguards is challenging, and many papers do not require this, but we encourage authors to take this into account and make a best faith effort.

  56. 12.

    Licenses for existing assets

  57. Question: Are the creators or original owners of assets (e.g., code, data, models), used in the paper, properly credited and are the license and terms of use explicitly mentioned and properly respected?

  58. Answer: [Yes]

  59. Justification: Section 2 cites the model reports, and Appendix E gives pinned revisions, model-card URLs, and the Qwen Research and MIT licenses.

  60. Guidelines:

    • •

      The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not use existing assets.

    • •

      The authors should cite the original paper that produced the code package or dataset.

    • •

      The authors should state which version of the asset is used and, if possible, include a URL.

    • •

      The name of the license (e.g., CC-BY 4.0) should be included for each asset.

    • •

      For scraped data from a particular source (e.g., website), the copyright and terms of service of that source should be provided.

    • •

      If assets are released, the license, copyright information, and terms of use in the package should be provided. For popular datasets, paperswithcode.com/datasets has curated licenses for some datasets. Their licensing guide can help determine the license of a dataset.

    • •

      For existing datasets that are re-packaged, both the original license and the license of the derived asset (if it has changed) should be provided.

    • •

      If this information is not available online, the authors are encouraged to reach out to the asset’s creators.

  61. 13.

    New assets

  62. Question: Are new assets introduced in the paper well documented and is the documentation provided alongside the assets?

  63. Answer: [N/A]

  64. Justification: No new dataset or model is released with the anonymous submission; the paper describes a synthetic experimental artifact that will be released after review.

  65. Guidelines:

    • •

      The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not release new assets.

    • •

      Researchers should communicate the details of the dataset/code/model as part of their submissions via structured templates. This includes details about training, license, limitations, etc.

    • •

      The paper should discuss whether and how consent was obtained from people whose asset is used.

    • •

      At submission time, remember to anonymize your assets (if applicable). You can either create an anonymized URL or include an anonymized zip file.

  66. 14.

    Crowdsourcing and research with human subjects

  67. Question: For crowdsourcing experiments and research with human subjects, does the paper include the full text of instructions given to participants and screenshots, if applicable, as well as details about compensation (if any)?

  68. Answer: [N/A]

  70. Guidelines:

    • •

      The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not involve crowdsourcing nor research with human subjects.

    • •

      Including this information in the supplemental material is fine, but if the main contribution of the paper involves human subjects, then as much detail as possible should be included in the main paper.

      According to the NeurIPS Code of Ethics, workers involved in data collection, curation, or other labor should be paid at least the minimum wage in the country of the data collector.

  71. 15.

    Institutional review board (IRB) approvals or equivalent for research with human subjects

  72. Question: Does the paper describe potential risks incurred by study participants, whether such risks were disclosed to the subjects, and whether Institutional Review Board (IRB) approvals (or an equivalent approval/review based on the requirements of your country or institution) were obtained?

  73. Answer: [N/A]

    • •

      The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not involve crowdsourcing nor research with human subjects.

    • •

      Depending on the country in which research is conducted, IRB approval (or equivalent) may be required for any human subjects research. If you obtained IRB approval, you should clearly state this in the paper.
